title: Cannabis-Specific Workplace Exposures and Emergency Escalation

content.overview: Cannabis work can involve respiratory, allergic, chemical, physical and ergonomic exposures. Learners practice recognizing warning signs and choosing the correct routine, safety or emergency escalation path.

vocabulary.definition: A process in which repeated exposure can lead the immune system to react strongly to a substance.
Airborne plant-derived dust or particles that may irritate or sensitize workers.
Transfer of a condition to a person or team with the authority and competence to manage it.

sections.title: Recognize cannabis-work exposures
sections.body: NIOSH identifies potential cannabis-work exposures including carbon dioxide, pesticides, ozone, plant allergens, microbes, endotoxins, organic particulate, heat, noise, ultraviolet light, repetitive work and general safety hazards. Site-specific assessment determines which controls apply.

sections.title: Report symptoms and alarms
sections.body: NIOSH has documented concern about work-related asthma and allergic symptoms in cannabis production. Workers should follow workplace reporting and medical procedures for respiratory, skin or eye symptoms and should obey emergency procedures for alarms such as unsafe gas conditions rather than self-diagnosing or entering to investigate without authorization.

workedExamples: Recurring breathing difficulty associated with dusty work is reported through the workplace health and safety process instead of being ignored.
A CO2 alarm triggers the posted emergency procedure rather than an unauthorized room entry.
commonMistakes: Assuming natural plant material cannot cause occupational allergy or asthma.
Entering an alarmed space to investigate without authorization.
content.practicalApplication: Classify exposure scenarios as continue with controls, pause/correct, stop/escalate, or emergency response and identify what should be documented.
content.summary: Cannabis cultivation has recognizable occupational exposures. Technicians follow controls, report symptoms and unsafe conditions, and use the correct escalation route.

blocks.title: Natural does not mean nonhazardous
blocks.body: Cannabis plant material and cultivation work can involve organic particulate, allergens, microbes, pesticides, carbon dioxide, ozone, heat, noise, ultraviolet light, repetitive work, and other facility-specific exposures. The presence and level of risk vary by task and workplace, so site-specific assessment and controls matter.

blocks.alt: Simplified cultivation room showing irrigation water approaching damaged electrical equipment, a blocked aisle, an unstable ladder, an exposed cutting tool, high-intensity lighting, and a carbon-dioxide life-safety alarm, with a reminder to scan for other task-specific exposures.
blocks.caption: A visual room scan should include both ordinary workplace hazards and exposures that can be prominent in cultivation work.

blocks.title: Exposure categories and technician response
rows: Plant dust, organic particulate, allergens, microbes
Use assessed controls, report symptoms or failures, and escalate when conditions exceed the procedure.
Cleaning chemicals, pesticides where applicable, ozone or other process chemicals
Use current label/SDS and site controls; do not improvise exposure controls.
Heat, intense light/UV, noise, slips, falls, ladders
Apply authorized routine controls and stop/escalate uncontrolled conditions.
Carbon-dioxide enrichment or other monitored gas conditions
Treat alarms as action signals and follow the posted emergency procedure.
Repetitive hand work, awkward handling, material movement
Use approved work practices and report conditions or symptoms that require review.

blocks.title: Report patterns; do not self-diagnose
blocks.body: Recurring cough, wheeze, chest tightness, shortness of breath, eye irritation, skin reactions, or other symptoms associated with work should be reported through the workplace health and safety process. Medical diagnosis belongs to qualified health professionals.

blocks.title: Symptoms only during a dusty task
blocks.setting: A worker reports coughing and chest tightness that appear during one dusty dry-plant handling task. A coworker suggests grabbing any available dust mask and continuing.
blocks.prompt: What is the stronger Technician I response?
options: Continue because the symptoms stop after the task
Use any available mask without checking the program
Report the work-related symptom pattern and verify the assessed controls and required PPE for the task
Move faster so exposure time is shorter
blocks.answer: Report the work-related symptom pattern and verify the assessed controls and required PPE for the task.
blocks.feedback: Work-related respiratory symptoms warrant reporting and evaluation through the workplace process. Improvised respiratory protection may be ineffective and can fall outside the worker's authority or the employer's respiratory-protection program.

blocks.title: Alarms are action signals, not diagnosis invitations
blocks.body: A carbon-dioxide or other life-safety alarm should trigger the posted response procedure. If you are not assigned emergency-response duties, do not enter an unsafe or alarmed area simply to check a controller or see whether the condition feels normal.

blocks.title: Exposure and escalation sort
blocks.instructions: Classify each supplied case as continue with controls, pause/correct, stop/escalate, or emergency response. Record the observation that drove the classification and what information should be handed off.
prompts: Plant dust is visible during a task and the assigned local-control equipment is not operating.
A life-safety gas alarm activates in an enriched room.
A worker reports repeated skin irritation associated with one handling task.
A cart blocks a marked route but can be moved using the normal procedure.
A chemical container is present but the product identity cannot be confirmed.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Cultivation-specific competence is not memorizing a list of hazards. It is recognizing meaningful conditions, using the site's assessed controls, reporting symptoms and failures accurately, and selecting the correct escalation route when routine work is no longer controlled.
